581.quote_or_event: “Knowledge is fivefold: 1. Sruta, knowledge derived from the sacred books; 2. Âbhinibôdhika, perception; 3. Avadhi, supernatural knowledge; 4. Manahparyâya, knowledge of the thoughts of other people; 5. Kêvala, the highest, unlimited knowledge.”
581.explanation: Jain epistemology begins its list of the ways of knowing with two ordinary sources: what is learned from scripture (śruta) and what is learned by direct observation (mati or perception).
581.tie_back: The Kural's two eyes, the law-books that show what ought to be done and the spies who report what is actually happening, line up with scripture-knowledge and perception, the first two Jain kinds of knowledge.
581.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 28.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
581._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified). The pairing of scripture and observation is a real structural parallel, but the Jain list is about the soul's knowing, not statecraft, and it has five members rather than two.

582.quote_or_event: “He was a Kevalin, omniscient and comprehending all objects, he knew all conditions of the world, of gods, men, and demons; whence they come, where they go … their food, drink, doings, desires, open and secret deeds, their conversation and gossip, and the thoughts of their minds; he saw and knew all conditions in the whole world of all living beings.”
582.explanation: On attaining kevala-jñāna Mahavira is described as knowing everything about every being, including their hidden deeds and thoughts, at all times.
582.tie_back: The Kural asks the king to know everything that happens to everyone, at all times; Jainism places that complete, all-encompassing knowledge in the omniscient Jina rather than in any ruler or his spies.
582.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra 2.15.26 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; wisdomlib.org)
582._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi's translation on wisdomlib.org (ellipsis marks an omitted clause). The 'all persons, all things, all times' scope matches well, but Jain omniscience is the soul's own perfected knowledge, not intelligence gathered by agents.

583.quote_or_event: “Without (right) faith there is no (right) knowledge, without (right) knowledge there is no virtuous conduct, without virtues there is no deliverance, and without deliverance there is no perfection.”
583.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana makes right knowledge a precondition of right conduct, and right conduct a precondition of final success.
583.tie_back: As the Kural says a king who does not gather and understand reports has no path to victory, Jainism says that without correct knowledge there is no way to the soul's victory.
583.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 28.30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
583._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The logic of 'no knowledge, no success' is shared, but the Jain victory is liberation, not conquest, and the knowledge in view is doctrinal, not intelligence.

584.quote_or_event: “Though others sleep, be thou awake! Like a wise man, trust nobody, but be always on the alert; for dangerous is the time and weak the body. Be always watchful like a Bhârunda bird!”
584.explanation: Mahavira's sermon on carelessness tells the monk to stay vigilant and not rely on anyone, comparing him to the mythical Bhāruṇḍa bird that is always on guard.
584.tie_back: The Kural's spy must watch officials, kin and enemies alike; this verse gives the same posture of universal, unsleeping watchfulness, though turned inward against spiritual danger.
584.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 4.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
584._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified). The 'trust nobody, stay alert' attitude fits, but the verse concerns a monk's vigilance against carelessness, not surveillance of others.

585.quote_or_event: “Living thus he with equanimity bore, endured, sustained, and suffered all calamities arising from divine powers, men, and animals, with undisturbed and unafflicted mind, careful of body, speech, and mind.”
585.explanation: During his twelve years as a wandering ascetic Mahavira met every hardship without being shaken, keeping strict guard over body, speech and mind.
585.tie_back: The Kural's spy does not flinch under anyone's gaze and never lets slip what he holds; Mahavira's unshaken composure and guarded speech give a Jain picture of that steadiness, though without any secret mission.
585.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra 2.15.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; wisdomlib.org)
585._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi's translation on wisdomlib.org. The parallel is in composure and control of speech; the Jain ideal is spiritual endurance, not keeping intelligence secrets, so the fit is partial.

586.quote_or_event: Jain tradition relates that early in his ascetic wanderings Mahavira came near the village of Corāka, where guards wary of thieves asked who he was. Bound by his vow of silence, he did not answer; the guards took him for a thief or spy, seized him and tormented him, until two women who knew him (Somā and Jayantī) came and had him freed, and the guards begged forgiveness.
586.explanation: The story shows how a silent wandering renunciant could be suspected of being a spy, and how Mahavira kept his silence even under torture.
586.tie_back: The Kural's spy goes about in a renunciant's guise and never gives himself away whatever is done to him; this Jain story turns the image round, showing a real ascetic who was mistaken for a spy and still revealed nothing under torment.
586.source: Life of Mahāvīra, episode at Corāka in his fourth year of ascetic practice (HereNow4U, 'Lord Śrī Mahāvīra', as summarised in the wisdomlib.org Jainism glossary s.v. Corāka)
586._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from a secondary Jain biography of Mahavira as cited on wisdomlib.org; I did not locate the primary passage (traditionally in the Āvaśyaka commentaries and Hemacandra's Mahāvīracaritra) in this session. Thematically vivid but inverted: Jainism forbids monks to act as spies.

587.quote_or_event: “(The excellence of faith depends on the following) eight points: 1. that one has no doubts (about the truth of the tenets); 2. that one has no preference (for heterodox tenets); 3. that one does not doubt its saving qualities …”
587.explanation: The first limb of right faith in Jainism (niḥśaṅkita) is freedom from doubt about what has been rightly understood.
587.tie_back: The Kural's ideal spy is left with no doubt about what he has found; Jainism likewise prizes conviction free of doubt as the first mark of sound understanding.
587.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 28.31 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
587._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (quotation truncated). Only the 'no doubt' half of the Kural is matched, and the Jain point concerns faith in doctrine, not certainty about gathered intelligence.

588.quote_or_event: Samantabhadra opens his Āptamīmāṃsā (also called Devāgamastotra) by refusing to accept even the Jina as an authority because of outward signs such as the arrival of gods, travel through the sky or royal fans, since such marvels are also seen among magicians; he then tests the Jina's teaching by reason and the logic of anekāntavāda before accepting it.
588.explanation: This classic Digambara work makes critical examination the ground for trust, even toward the most authoritative source.
588.tie_back: The Kural says even a trusted spy's report must be re-checked by another spy before it is accepted; Samantabhadra applies the same rule of verification to the highest authority Jainism recognises.
588.source: Samantabhadra, Āptamīmāṃsā (Devāgamastotra) v. 1 and overall argument (described in Vijay K. Jain's translation, 2016; PhilArchive record)
588._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the content of verse 1 is a well-known opening, and the work's method of testing the omniscient by reason is confirmed in the publisher's description on PhilArchive. I did not read the verse in translation this session. Good fit on 'verify before trusting', different domain.

589.quote_or_event: “He who understands the true nature of all substances by means of all proofs (pramâna) and nayas, believes by a complete course of study.”
589.explanation: Jain epistemology holds that a thing is properly known only when it is examined through valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and from several partial standpoints (naya), which are then brought together.
589.tie_back: The Kural trusts a matter only when three independent spies' reports agree; the Jain method likewise reaches confidence by combining several separate lines of evidence and viewpoint rather than relying on one.
589.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 28.24 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
589._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified). The parallel is only general (many sources, one conclusion); nothing in Jain texts I found matches the specific rule of three mutually unknown agents.

590.quote_or_event: “the divulging from jealousy or other motives of the secret intention of another person as divined by watching his gestures or facial expression”
590.explanation: Among the faults that break the layperson's vow of truthfulness (Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.26) is sākāra-mantrabheda; the Digambara interpretation reproduced here defines it as exposing a secret read from outward signs, and Siddhasena's commentary links a related fault to 'divulging affairs of state'.
590.tie_back: The Kural warns that a king who honours a spy in public betrays the secret through an outward sign; Jain ethics names the leaking of hidden matters through visible signs as a breach of the truth vow.
590.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.26, sākāra-mantrabheda, Digambara interpretation (Cāmuṇḍarāya's Cāritrasāra) as given in R. Williams, Jaina Yoga (1963), quoted in the wisdomlib.org Jainism glossary
590._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the wisdomlib.org glossary entry quoting Williams' Jaina Yoga. The concern with secrets leaked through visible signs is a genuine match, but in Jainism the fault lies in exposing another's secret, not in a ruler carelessly revealing his own.
